newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right leads in voters' election hopes.
newsitem.headline: French right leads in voters' election hopes.

text.p: A narrow plurality of French voters hope the conservatives will retain power in a snap parliamentary election on May 25-June 1, acording to an opinion poll released on Wednesday.

The Ifop poll, carried out for the weekly magazine VSD last Saturday -- two days before President Jacques Chirac dissolved parliament -- found 42 percent wanted the ruling centre-right to win, to 38 percent who hoped for a left-wing victory. Twenty percent had no opinion.

Twenty-four percent said they wanted Edouard Balladur, who was prime minister from 1993 to 1995, when he lost the presidential election to fellow-Gaullist Chirac, to return to the premiership if the conservatives won.
Unpopular Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe came only fourth on the list of preferred conservative candidates for premier, polling 11 per cent.
Outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, who advocates giving precedence to the fight against unemployment over strict compliance with Maastricht Treaty budget criteria, polled 23 percent.
Ultra-liberal ex-finance minister Alain Madelin was preferred by 13 percent.
On the Left, voters made Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin the number two choice for prime minister, behind ex-labour minister Martine Aubry.
Jospin who is leading the election campaign polled 22 percent to 24 percent for Aubry, the daughter of former European Commmisison president Jacques Delors.
A majority of 58 percent favoured power-sharing between Chirac and a left-wing prime minister if the Left won, to 31 percent who opposed it.

The late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand had to share power with a conservative premier in 1986-88 and 1993-95 but a left-wing victory would produce the first "cohabitation" between a conservative president and a left-wing prime minister.
The poll was conducted with a standard sample of 1,002 adults.
